summary: A 1935 CCC steel lookout in Sampson County, sold at a 2018 state surplus auction and taken down for a private farm in Wilkes County.

facts.status_note: Taken down in 2018 and sold; no source confirms it was reassembled.

access.note: Bought by a private family in 2018; their reported plan was to reassemble it on their farm in McGrady, Wilkes County.

facts.agency: North Carolina Division of Forest Resources

events.note: CCC erected the steel tower for $1,423.80; a 2018 newspaper gives 1936
CCC Camp P-68 completed a four-room frame house at the tower
Surplus auction opened 22 March 2018; the tower was taken down and bought by a private family

evidence.supports: CCC erected 99-foot 9-inch steel tower, November 1935, $1,423.80
evidence.quote: November 1935: The Civilian Conservation Corps erected a 99-foot 9-inch steel tower costing $1,423.80.

evidence.supports: funding through Emergency Conservation Works program
evidence.quote: The funding was through the Emergency Conservation Works program.

evidence.supports: height 99 ft from platform to top; built 1936
evidence.quote: From the bottom of the platform to the top, the height is 99 feet. It was built in 1936 and was a landmark in the community, up until Friday.

evidence.supports: beside Fire Tower Road; bought for $384 at surplus auction
evidence.quote: Larry and Beth Horrell purchased the tower next to Fire Tower Road for $384 through a surplus and auction process from the State of North Carolina.

evidence.supports: Harrells location
evidence.quote: HARRELLS — While wearing hardhats, the Horrell family looked up towards the Newkirk Fire Tower

evidence.supports: CCC Camp P-68 frame house completed 1939
evidence.quote: 4-room frame house at Newkirk tower in Sampson County; completed July 28, 1939 by Camp P-68.

evidence.supports: fold-down map case with magnets for fires
evidence.quote: After climbing to the top, there was a fold-down map case of the surrounding area, with magnets to mark fires.

evidence.supports: operators watched for smoke with an azimuth wheel
evidence.quote: an operator would climb to the top to look for smoke using an azimuth wheel

evidence.supports: ranger remark on fires found by operators
evidence.quote: There’s no telling how many fires these operators in this tower have found

evidence.supports: bidding on surplus state property opened 22 March 2018
evidence.quote: March 22, 2018: Auction was opened for bid on the surplus state property.

evidence.supports: tower on state property; reversion clause requires removal
evidence.quote: The tower is located on State property, however, a reversion clause in the deed requires the tower be removed when no longer used for its original function.

evidence.supports: move and take-down cost $2,000
evidence.quote: The expense to take it down and move it was $2,000.

evidence.supports: plan to reassemble on 50-acre farm in McGrady, Wilkes County
evidence.quote: The Horrells plan to take the pieces back home to McGrady, a community in Wilkes County. It will be reassembled on their 50 acre farm.

evidence.supports: blog gives sale year as 2021
evidence.quote: Sold to a private citizen in 2021 and moved out of the county

evidence.supports: blog says tower named for William King Newkirk
evidence.quote: Named for County Forest Warden William King Newkirk (1909–1982)

evidence.supports: 2018 newspaper article date
dismantling began; completion planned
evidence.quote: With help, they began dismantling it Monday with plans to finish before Saturday.

evidence.supports: agency is North Carolina Division of Forest Resources
evidence.quote: North Carolina Division of Forest Resources

evidence.supports: Sampson County ranger named as Grant Jones
evidence.quote: Grant Jones, Sampson County Ranger for the North Carolina Forest Service

evidence.supports: GPS and cell-phone remark; operators looked for smoke with an azimuth wheel
evidence.quote: Before technology such as GPS, satellites in the sky, and cell phones, an operator would climb to the top to look for smoke using an azimuth wheel

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The state report quoted on the Forest Lookouts page gives November 1935; the 2018 newspaper says 1936. The story uses the 1935 state date and reports both.
The 1935 entry gives 99 ft 9 in (30.4 m); the 2018 newspaper gives 99 ft (30.2 m) from platform to top. The record's 30.2 m follows the newspaper.
A genealogy blog gives 2021 for the sale; the 2018 auction notice and the 2018 newspaper support 2018, which the story follows.

sources.title: Newkirk Fire Tower – Harrells, North Carolina

notes_for_editor: Built year (1935 state entry, 1936 newspaper) and sale year (2018 auction and newspaper, 2021 blog) disagree; the story says so. The McGrady reassembly is a 2018 plan with no later confirmation, and no source describes the Harrells site now. Record status was unknown; facts now say removed. The 2018 auction notice was read only through the Forest Lookouts page, which quotes mcstatesurplus.com. The blog's naming claim is attributed to it and not checked. No photos added.
